record.original_question: Improve the comparison table between quadratic polynomial systems and piecewise linear systems with a straight separation line by determining the best possible values for: maximum number of limit cycles, maximum number of algebraic limit cycles, maximum number of non-hyperbolic algebraic limit cycles, whether algebraic and non-algebraic limit cycles can coexist, and the maximum number of critical periods.

evidence.quote: Problem 17. Improve this table: Quadratic sys. / Piecewise linear sys.; Limit cycles 4? / 3?; Algebraic limit cycles 1? / 2?; Non hyperbolic algebraic l.c. 0? / 1?; Coex. of algebraic and non-algebraic l.c. NO? / NO; Critical periods 2? / ?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider two classes of planar polynomial differential systems on $\mathbb{R}^2$:

(A) Quadratic polynomial systems
$$\dot{x}=P(x,y),\qquad \dot{y}=Q(x,y),$$
where $P,Q\in\mathbb{R}[x,y]$ have $\max(\deg P,\deg Q)=2$.

(B) Piecewise linear differential systems with two zones separated by a straight line: after an affine change of coordinates the separation line is $\Sigma=\{x=0\}$, and the system is given by
$$(\dot{x},\dot{y})=\begin{cases} (a_1 x+b_1 y+c_1,\ d_1 x+e_1 y+f_1), & x>0,\\ (a_2 x+b_2 y+c_2,\ d_2 x+e_2 y+f_2), & x<0,\end{cases}$$
with Filippov convention on $\Sigma$.

A limit cycle is an isolated periodic orbit of the system (in case (B), an isolated closed trajectory in the Filippov sense which may cross $\Sigma$). An algebraic limit cycle is a limit cycle contained in the zero set of an irreducible real polynomial that is invariant under the flow (in case (B), invariant in each zone). An algebraic limit cycle $\gamma$ given by $\{f(x,y)=0\}$ is hyperbolic if its associated cofactor does not vanish identically along $\gamma$ in the appropriate sense; otherwise it is non-hyperbolic. A critical period of a center is a critical point of the period function on the punctured period annulus.

For each class (A) and (B), determine the sharp (best possible) values of the following five quantities:

1. The maximum number of limit cycles.
2. The maximum number of algebraic limit cycles.
3. The maximum number of non-hyperbolic algebraic limit cycles.
4. Whether algebraic and non-algebraic limit cycles can coexist in the same system (yes/no).
5. The maximum number of critical periods.

The currently conjectured values to be improved are: for (A), $4$, $1$, $0$, no, $2$; for (B), $3$, $2$, $1$, no, unknown.
artifact.category_tag: Limit cycles of planar differential systems
artifact.status_search_result: All five quantities, in both the quadratic polynomial and the piecewise linear (one straight separation line) settings, remain open. Even the maximum number of limit cycles is unsettled: for piecewise linear systems with one straight line of separation, the longstanding conjectured upper bound is 3 (with examples reaching 3) but no proof of sharpness exists; for quadratic systems the Hilbert number $H(2)$ is famously unknown (at least 4). Recent works continue to improve bounds and constructions, but the precise sharp values for algebraic limit cycles, non-hyperbolic algebraic limit cycles, coexistence, and critical periods are not established.

status_evidence.title: On the number of limit cycles in discontinuous piecewise linear differential systems with two pieces separated by a straight line
status_evidence.snippet: Studies the still-open problem of the maximum number of limit cycles for two-zone piecewise linear systems with a straight line of separation; the conjectured maximum is 3.
status_evidence.claim: The maximum number of limit cycles for piecewise linear systems with two zones separated by a straight line is conjectured but not proven to be 3.

status_evidence.title: On the number of limit cycles in piecewise planar quadratic differential systems
status_evidence.snippet: Determining an analogue of the Hilbert number for piecewise polynomial systems is the heart of present research; sharp values are not known.
status_evidence.claim: Sharp bounds on limit cycles for quadratic and piecewise systems remain open active research.
